stories.brief: Curt Wormann’s role in professionalizing and internationalizing Israeli librarianship.

sources.title: Book Diplomacy: Curt Wormann and the International Librarians

storyBeats: Curt David Wormann was a Berlin-trained librarian who worked in public librarianship before emigrating to Palestine in the 1930s.
After arriving in Israel, he worked in Tel Aviv municipal librarianship and later became involved with the Jewish National and University Library and the Hebrew University.
By the first years of statehood, Wormann emerged as one of the people pushing Israeli librarianship away from ad hoc practice and toward a more formal professional system.
The Curt David Wormann archive preserves material on his work as a pioneer of Israeli librarianship, including the founding of the school of librarianship in Jerusalem.
The NLI archive list explicitly describes him as a pioneer of Israeli librarianship and notes that he founded the school of librarianship in Jerusalem.
Wormann used UNESCO membership and international contacts as a route to connect Israeli librarianship with wider professional networks during the early decades of the state.

Those efforts also served domestic institutional goals, including strengthening the standing of the Jewish National and University Library during a period when parts of its collections remained on Mount Scopus.
A 1964 UNESCO seminar file preserved in his archive includes his lecture drafts on cooperation between national libraries and libraries in other countries.

The archive and accompanying NLI materials frame Wormann as an agent of the internationalization, professionalization, and institutionalization of Israeli librarianship rather than as a mere manager of a library collection.

stories.brief: Tnuva as a long-running Israeli dairy cooperative turned major food company.
storyBeats: Tnuva was founded in 1926 as a cooperative marketing arrangement created by leaders of the kibbutz movement.
Its original purpose was to distribute and export agricultural products from the collective farming sector, especially dairy goods.
In 1946, the founders decided to open a joint factory in Bnei Brak after previously operating separate noodle factories.
Over time Tnuva moved beyond a cooperative distribution network and grew into a dominant national food manufacturer, with dairy at the center of its business.
Early branding and advertisements tied Tnuva products to everyday Israeli life and to the kibbutz-based economy that produced them.
The company expanded from milk distribution into additional food lines, eventually becoming one of Israel’s largest food manufacturers.
The company’s ownership later changed from cooperative control to corporate control after its sale and restructuring.
Tnuva remains a central name in Israel’s food system, with its history presented as a key part of the country’s agricultural and industrial development.

stories.brief: Hebrew folksong research and educational forums as part of Israeli musical culture history.

sources.title: The Music Collection and Sound Archive

storyBeats: Tsippi Fleischer began studying Hebrew song as a teenager and treated it as a field for historical and educational research.
Her 1964 high-school project, The Historical Development of the Hebrew Folksong, examined the history of Hebrew song in broad scope and was described as the first study of its kind in Israel.
That study was later recognized as a serious ethnomusicological work and eventually published as a substantial book.
The published work surveyed songs from the pioneering settlement period, the pre-state transition, and the early years of the state, and included interviews and musical analysis.
From 1992 to 1996, Fleischer carried out the Hebrew Song Forums project at Levinsky College of Education.
The forums turned Hebrew folksong from a research topic into an organized educational practice that combined student participation, performance, and teaching.
The project led to open concerts at the college on the pioneers of folksong and musical education in the Jewish Yishuv.
Fleischer also built teaching materials around Hebrew song as an interdisciplinary tool that connected music with history, society, and literature.
By the time of the NLI profile, the Hebrew Song Forums were presented as an influential model for performers, educators, and arrangers across Israel.

stories.brief: Early visual documentation of the Bank of Israel and the state’s financial institutions.
storyBeats: After statehood, Israel needed a central bank to manage monetary policy, credit, and the banking system of a young and fragile economy.
In 1951 the government created a committee to study central banks abroad and develop the plan for a state bank in Israel.
The Bank of Israel Law was approved by the Knesset in August 1954 and took effect on 1 December 1954.
The Bank opened for business on 1 December 1954 in Jerusalem, and the official dedication ceremony followed later that month at the King David Hotel.
The Bank’s own historical pages preserve images and captions drawn from state and central archives, showing counting and sorting of notes among the early institutional imagery.
The Government Press Office describes its National Photography Collection as a visual history of the state, including material from before statehood and from Israel’s early years.
Over time the institution became a permanent national body, moving to its government complex home in Jerusalem in 1981.
The Bank of Israel now presents its own founding as part of the larger state-building story, with its archives and imagery anchoring that memory.

stories.brief: Osem’s growth from a 1940s food company into one of Israel’s largest manufacturers.

sources.title: Every Shabbat, Osem Advertisement | Primary Sources

storyBeats: Osem was founded in 1942 as a joint marketing body for Israeli pasta manufacturers.
The company began with seven food-industry founders who pooled production and sales rather than competing separately.
In 1946, the founders opened a joint factory in Bnei Brak, turning the marketing alliance into a more integrated manufacturing operation.
The company expanded from noodle marketing into broader food production and distribution as Israel’s food economy grew.
Osem became closely associated with immigrant absorption, regional development, and the rise of Israeli industrial manufacturing.
The company’s own history page presents its story as intertwined with the state’s development since 1942.
Its product portfolio and distribution footprint later widened enough for Osem to become one of Israel’s largest food manufacturers.
By the modern period, Osem was operating as a major branded food group rather than a narrow cooperative venture.

stories.brief: Israeli food culture during the austerity years and the early cookbook tradition.

sources.title: The Book That Taught Europeans How to Cook in Palestine

storyBeats: Early Israeli cuisine developed under conditions of immigration, scarcity, and the need to adapt European food habits to local ingredients.
In the 1930s, cookbooks such as How to Cook in Palestine taught new arrivals how to cook with local produce, vegetable oil, spices, and electricity.
Those early books tried to replace European kitchen habits with recipes suited to the climate and available ingredients of the Land of Israel.
After statehood, food rationing and shortages became a defining public condition in the 1950s austerity years.
The austerity system included rationing and a constrained daily diet, shaping what households could buy and cook.
Cooks responded by developing dishes that stretched scarce ingredients and adapted familiar tastes to the shortages of the time.
The National Library’s food pages highlight dishes such as eggplant-based substitutes and other attempts to preserve a recognizable taste under rationing.
By the early state period, Israeli food culture had taken shape through a combination of cookbook experimentation, rationing, and immigrant adaptation.

Yossi Banai as a key Israeli stage and song figure whose language and performances shaped popular culture.
storyBeats: Yossi Banai was born in Jerusalem in 1932 into a large family that produced several figures in Israeli culture.
He served in the Nahal entertainment troupe and then studied acting at the Habima studio, moving into professional stage work.
Banai then went to Paris, where chanson culture shaped the direction of his later work as a writer, singer, and stage performer.
After returning to Israel, he performed in landmark shows such as Tel Aviv HaKtana and built a reputation in solo performance and satire.
In 1963 he founded the Seasons Theater with Avner Hezkyahu and Nissim Aloni.
The Seasons Theater became a vehicle for major Aloni productions, linking Banai’s name to influential modern Israeli stage work.
Alongside theatre, Banai wrote and performed songs that became part of the Israeli repertoire and appeared in film and television.
His archive at the National Library preserves the breadth of his work across theatre, song, and public performance.
Banai received the Israel Prize for theatre in 1998 and became recognized as one of Israel’s most important stage artists.

A couple at home is deciding what to bring to Sunday lunch with friends. They compare two simple desserts they can make quickly, notice one is already too rich for the main meal, and discuss whether to keep it light or add a small extra topping. One person says they do not have much time, so they choose the easier recipe and save the second option for another day. They finish the dessert, write down the adjusted ingredients, and leave the kitchen with a clear plan and no extra shopping.
